predictions.explanation:
Available national data through late 2025 show *no large, broad nominal decline* in U.S. home prices relative to their 2022 peak; instead, prices have generally kept rising, albeit more slowly.

- The FHFA House Price Index reports that U.S. house prices have shown **positive annual appreciation every quarter since 2012**, including 2023–2025, with prices up 6.6% year‑over‑year in Q1 2024 and 4.0% year‑over‑year in Q1 2025.([fhfa.gov](https://www.fhfa.gov/news/news-release/u.s.-house-prices-rise-6.6-percent-over-the-last-year-up-1.1-percent-from-the-fourth-quarter-of-2023?utm_source=openai)) 
- S&P CoreLogic Case‑Shiller data show that the **national index hit new all‑time highs multiple times in 2023 and 2024** and again in March–April 2024, explicitly noting that prices have surpassed the prior 2022 peak.([press.spglobal.com](https://press.spglobal.com/2024-02-27-S-P-CORELOGIC-CASE-SHILLER-INDEX-REPORTS-5-5-ANNUAL-HOME-PRICE-GAIN-FOR-CALENDAR-2023?utm_source=openai)) 
- By mid‑ to late‑2025, both FHFA and Case‑Shiller still show **positive year‑over‑year national price increases**, even as growth slows and some individual metros (e.g., parts of the West and certain Sunbelt cities) remain below their local 2022 highs or see modest declines.([fhfa.gov](https://www.fhfa.gov/news/news-release/u.s.-house-prices-rise-2.2-percent-year-over-year-up-0.2-percent-quarter-over-quarter?utm_source=openai))

So far, the evidence contradicts the *substance* of a "big" nationwide nominal correction below 2022 levels. However, Sacks’ timeframe was "as [higher rates] wash through the system" over the "subsequent few years" after mid‑2023. As of November 2025 we are only about 2½ years into that loosely defined window, and a sizable downturn *could* still occur before a reasonable "few years" horizon (≈3–4 years) fully elapses. Because the prediction has clearly **not yet come true** but also **cannot yet be definitively ruled out** on its own stated timeline, the fairest scoring at this point is **inconclusive (too early)**.

predictions.explanation:
David Sacks’ core claim was that, by 2024–2025, **multifamily would shift from a “safe” asset to one in clear, broad-based distress, especially for borrowers needing to refinance**, and that distress would be of the same general order as what was already visible in office.

By mid‑2024, industry data started to describe **multifamily as a sector “in distress”**. CRED iQ/Trepp analyses cited in July 2024 showed delinquencies and special‑servicing rates for multifamily CMBS and CRE‑CLO loans up about **185% in the first half of 2024**, with **over 7% of multifamily CMBS loans and nearly 10% of CRE‑CLOs distressed**, and roughly **35% of multifamily loans maturing within about 18 months**, making refinancing at much higher rates a central problem. ([ctol.digital](https://www.ctol.digital/news/multifamily-real-estate-sector-in-distress/?utm_source=openai))  A separate CRED iQ analysis found multifamily distress accelerating into late 2024 and early 2025, with distress characterized as a **systemic issue** across lenders rather than isolated to a few properties. ([chicagodealflow.com](https://www.chicagodealflow.com/pages/warning-multifamily-loan-distress-hits-12-year-high-what-smart-investors-must-know-now?utm_source=openai))  Fortune likewise estimated around **$95 billion of U.S. multifamily properties already in distress or at risk**, noting that many floating‑rate, 3‑year loans were now underwater and facing refi challenges. ([fortune.com](https://fortune.com/2024/09/01/commercial-real-estate-debt-1-5-trillion-due-by-refinancing-apartments-interest-rates/?utm_source=openai))

By 2025, **measured distress in multifamily was high and still rising**. Trepp’s CMBS data (via Multi‑Housing News and Multifamily Dive) show multifamily CMBS delinquency jumping from roughly **1.3–1.8% in 2024 to the mid‑single digits by early 2025**, with April 2025 delinquencies around **6.6% on a CMBS basis, or ~8.4% if you include loans past maturity but still paying**, and CRED iQ putting **overall multifamily distress at ~13%**, second only to office. ([multihousingnews.com](https://www.multihousingnews.com/2025-cmbs-delinquency-rates/?utm_source=openai))  Through August–October 2025, Trepp/CRE Daily report multifamily CMBS delinquencies around **6.9–7.1%, the highest in nearly a decade**, while stressing that multifamily has become one of the two most troubled property types in CMBS alongside office. ([credaily.com](https://www.credaily.com/briefs/cmbs-delinquency-climbs-amid-office-and-multifamily-woes/?utm_source=openai))  That is exactly the kind of **elevated defaults and loan trouble** Sacks was talking about.

Sacks also emphasized that *any* real‑estate developer needing financing in the following “year or two” would face distress. Broad CRE data back up that **refinancing pressure became pervasive across property types**: a 2025 overview notes nearly **$1 trillion of CRE loans maturing in 2025 alone—roughly triple the 20‑year average—creating “unprecedented refinancing pressure”**, with CMBS delinquency rates above 7% and rising. ([kaplancollectionagency.com](https://www.kaplancollectionagency.com/business-advice/is-commercial-real-estate-at-a-breaking-point-in-2025/?utm_source=openai))  This aligns with his claim that developers facing 2023–2025 maturities would generally be under stress, not just in office.

On the **comparison to office**: office clearly remains worse in absolute terms—office CMBS delinquencies reached **~11–12% in 2024–2025**, versus **~6–7% for multifamily**, and office vacancies near 20% make it the most impaired segment. ([multihousingnews.com](https://www.multihousingnews.com/2024-multifamily-cmbs-delinquency-rates/?utm_source=openai))  However, by 2025 industry commentary consistently describes multifamily as the **second‑most distressed major asset class, “not far behind” office** and at its own decade‑high delinquency and distress levels. ([multifamilydive.com](https://www.multifamilydive.com/news/trepp-crediq-cmbs-loans-deliquencies/745178/?utm_source=openai))  In other words, while office is still the epicenter, multifamily did in fact move into *material, broad‑based distress* rather than remaining a relatively unscathed safe haven.

The main nuance is that **distress has shown up first and most clearly in the capital stack (delinquencies, special servicing, underwater equity, maturity defaults)**; actual fire‑sale transaction volumes in multifamily have been more muted so far, and some REIT executives still say they see few bargain distressed deals in their specific markets. ([multifamilydive.com](https://www.multifamilydive.com/news/trepp-special-servicing-multifamily-deliquency-rates-cmbs/760284/?utm_source=openai))  But Sacks’ prediction was about financing stress, defaults, and impairment for borrowers needing to refinance, not necessarily about immediate mass liquidations. On that metric, the evidence shows that by 2024–2025 **multifamily refi borrowers as a group are indeed in significant distress, and that multifamily has joined office as a top problem sector**.

Given the timing and the scale of the documented problems, the prediction that *by 2025 multifamily would be clearly impaired and broadly distressed for borrowers needing refinancing, in a way comparable in seriousness (if not in exact percentages) to the office bust*, is substantially borne out by actual data. Hence the prediction is best classified as **right**.

predictions.explanation:
Chamath’s normalized prediction was that political pressure from widespread housing/real‑estate pain would cause the Fed to *start cutting rates earlier than the then‑prevailing market consensus for 2024 and beyond*.

1. **What the consensus was on Aug 18, 2023**  
   A Reuters poll of economists conducted Aug 14–18, 2023 (i.e., exactly when this episode was released) found:  
   * A strong majority thought the Fed was done hiking.  
   * Among 95 economists with forecasts through mid‑2024, **83% expected at least one rate cut by mid‑2024**, with views split between a first cut in Q1 2024 and Q2 2024.([thewealthadvisor.com](https://www.thewealthadvisor.com/article/fed-done-hiking-slim-majority-economists-say-no-rate-cut-through-march?utm_source=openai))  
   Separately, a Goldman Sachs research note dated Aug 13, 2023 projected the Fed would **start cutting in 2024 Q2** as inflation fell closer to target.([gspublishing.com](https://www.gspublishing.com/content/research/en/reports/2023/08/13/f9846a76-d6e5-45a8-83bf-24397656f500.html?utm_source=openai))  
   Together, these show that the mainstream expectation in mid‑August 2023 was for the first rate cut **by spring or early summer 2024**.

2. **What actually happened**  
   The Fed held the policy rate at 5.25–5.50% from July 2023 through mid‑September 2024. On **September 18, 2024** it delivered the first cut of the cycle, lowering the federal funds target range by 50 bps to **4.75–5.00%**.([cbre.com](https://www.cbre.com/insights/briefs/economic-watch-fed-makes-first-of-several-expected-rate-cuts?utm_source=openai))  
   This was the **first rate reduction since 2020**, and it arrived **several months later** than the Q1–Q2 2024 start that many economists and strategists had penciled in back in August 2023.([thewealthadvisor.com](https://www.thewealthadvisor.com/article/fed-done-hiking-slim-majority-economists-say-no-rate-cut-through-march?utm_source=openai))

3. **Did real‑estate pain clearly pull cuts *forward*?**  
   By 2023–24, commercial real estate and housing affordability were widely recognized problems, and industry groups openly argued higher rates were stressing real estate and community banks.([rer.org](https://www.rer.org/tag/federal-reserve/?utm_source=openai))  
   But when the Fed finally cut in September 2024, its own communications framed the move as a response to progress on inflation and emerging labor‑market weakness, not as an early, politically driven concession to property‑sector stress.([theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/business/live/2024/sep/18/us-interest-rate-decision-federal-reserve-uk-infation-cost-of-living-bank-of-england-business-live?utm_source=openai))  
   Moreover, by mid‑2024 the Fed’s *own* projections and public guidance had shifted to a “higher for longer” stance, signaling no rush to cut, and external forecasts had been revised toward **later**, not earlier, cuts.([wolfstreet.com](https://wolfstreet.com/2024/06/12/fed-sees-only-1-rate-cut-in-2024-holds-rates-at-5-50-top-of-range-qt-continues-at-slower-pace-as-announced-in-may/?utm_source=openai))

4. **Comparison to the prediction**  
   The falsifiable part of the normalized prediction is that rate cuts would **start sooner than the August 2023 consensus expected** because of political pressure from housing/real‑estate pain.  
   * Consensus in August 2023: first cut **by Q1–Q2 2024**.([thewealthadvisor.com](https://www.thewealthadvisor.com/article/fed-done-hiking-slim-majority-economists-say-no-rate-cut-through-march?utm_source=openai))  
   * Reality: first cut **September 18, 2024**, clearly **later** than that window.([cbre.com](https://www.cbre.com/insights/briefs/economic-watch-fed-makes-first-of-several-expected-rate-cuts?utm_source=openai))  
   There is no clear evidence that real‑estate distress caused the Fed to move *earlier* than it otherwise would have; if anything, the Fed delayed cuts relative to those earlier expectations.

Because the first rate cut came **later**, not earlier, than the then‑prevailing 2024 consensus, and there’s no strong evidence of an acceleration due to housing/real‑estate political pressure, the normalized prediction is best judged **wrong**.

predictions.explanation:
Evidence from 2024 supports Sacks’ core claim that cutting the short-term policy rate would *not* automatically bring down the 10-year yield or long-term real-estate borrowing costs.

Key facts:
- **Fed funds rate path (2024):** The Fed kept the target range at **5.25–5.5%** from July 2023 through the first part of 2024, then began easing, ending 2024 at **4.25–4.5%**—a noticeable series of cuts but still well above pre‑2022 levels and not as low as 3%. ([federalreserve.gov](https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/2024-03-mpr-part2.htm?utm_source=openai))
- **10-year Treasury remained elevated:** Monthly data show the 10‑year Treasury yield in mid‑to‑late 2024 running roughly **3.7–4.4%** (e.g., 4.31% in June, 4.25% in July, 3.87% in August, 3.72% in September, 4.10% in October, 4.36% in November, 4.39% in December). ([value-trades.com](https://value-trades.com/getTreasuryRate.php?utm_source=openai)) A commercial real-estate review using Treasury data reports an **average 10‑year yield of about 4.21% for 2024**, confirming that it stayed around the mid‑4% area on average rather than falling back to pre‑inflationary lows. ([etypeproductionstorage1.blob.core.windows.net](https://etypeproductionstorage1.blob.core.windows.net/%24web/Production_Prod/Jobs/702/2025-01-30/443738/FlippingBook/Colorado-Real-Estate-Journal_443738/index.html?utm_source=openai))
- **Mortgage/real-estate financing costs stayed high:** Bankrate’s 2024 recap notes 30‑year fixed mortgage rates mostly between **6.2% and 7.39%** during the year, starting near **6.9%** and ending around **7.0%**. ([bankrate.com](https://www.bankrate.com/mortgages/mortgage-rate-forecast/?utm_source=openai)) Freddie Mac–based weekly data show a similar band of roughly **6.1–7.2%** for 2024. ([propertycalcs.com](https://www.propertycalcs.com/historical-rates/rates/2024/30-year-mortgage/?utm_source=openai)) That is only a modest improvement from late‑2023 peaks and far from a return to the 3–4% mortgage environment—hard to describe as a “material” easing for long‑term real estate borrowers.
- **Disconnect between Fed cuts and mortgage rates:** Bankrate explicitly observes that after the Fed began cutting in 2024, **fixed mortgage rates actually rose**, underscoring that mortgage costs are driven more by the 10‑year yield and term premium than by the Fed’s short rate. ([bankrate.com](https://www.bankrate.com/mortgages/mortgage-rate-forecast/?utm_source=openai)) This is exactly the mechanism Sacks described (“no guarantee that the ten year rate will move down”).

The specific conditional detail that the Fed would cut *all the way* to 3–4% in 2024 did *not* occur, but that was framed as a hypothetical scenario. The falsifiable part of his prediction was the *relationship*: that even with easing in the policy rate, the 10‑year yield could remain elevated and long-term real-estate financing costs would not materially ease in 2024. Actual 2024 data show:

- Fed funds down modestly but still high,
- 10‑year yields hovering near ~4%+ on average, and
- Mortgage/real-estate borrowing costs remaining historically elevated.

On that substantive point, his prediction was borne out, so the best classification is **"right"**.

Consequently, 30-year mortgage rates remained elevated (~6.6% Jan to ~6.8% Dec, peaking 7.1% Oct; lingered in 6-7% range), showing no material easing ([Freddie Mac](https://www.freddiemac.com/pmms), [Macrotrends](https://www.macrotrends.net/2604/30-year-fixed-mortgage-rate-chart), [Bankrate](https://www.bankrate.com/mortgages/historical-mortgage-rates/)). predictions.explanation:
Evidence from 2023–2024 shows that U.S. real estate sponsors who *did* need to refinance were overwhelmingly forced into meaningfully worse debt structures—higher coupons, lower leverage, and/or extra credit support—relative to their prior loans, matching Sacks’s directional claim.

* **Rates far above legacy financing:** Many development and income properties had loans made in 2020–2021 at roughly 3–4%. By 2023–24, typical refi coupons had moved into the ~6.5–7% range, roughly doubling debt service costs for borrowers rolling maturing loans.([gcapitalfunding.com](https://gcapitalfunding.com/blog/how-to-handle-commercial-real-estate-debt--a-survival-guide-for-the--1-8t-crisis?utm_source=openai))  This is mechanically “worse terms” for almost any developer whose old financing was from the low‑rate era.
* **Systematic tightening on leverage and structure:** Industry pieces and lender commentary in 2023–24 describe banks and other lenders cutting maximum LTVs from around 75–80% toward ~60–65%, shortening loan terms, and requiring stronger DSCR and deposits/relationship business.([sior.com](https://www.sior.com/education-and-insights/insights/magazine/sior-report-article/fall-2024/the-tightening-up-of-lending?utm_source=openai))  Lower LTVs and stricter covenants mean developers either bring in substantial new equity or accept mezz/expensive capital—again clearly worse than the pre‑2022 environment.
* **Regulators and surveys confirm broad-based tightening:** The Federal Reserve’s January 2024 Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey reported that banks had recently tightened standards on CRE loans and that many expected further tightening over 2024; essentially no banks reported easing.([federalreserve.gov](https://www.federalreserve.gov/data/sloos/sloos-202401-table-2.htm?utm_source=openai))  That implies that, on average, new and refi CRE loans were being underwritten on tougher terms than legacy debt.
* **Refinancing stress was widespread, not isolated:** Analyses of the 2024 CRE “maturity wall” estimate on the order of $900–950B of U.S. CRE debt maturing in 2024 alone, much of it originated when rates were much lower and values higher. These reports describe many loans that *cannot* refinance “out of the box” without higher rates, new reserves, equity infusions, or other structural changes; some borrowers instead default, hand back keys, or accept short extensions with stricter conditions.([sterlingassetgroup.com](https://www.sterlingassetgroup.com/insights/us-commercial-real-estate-capital-markets-outlook-q3q4-2025?utm_source=openai))  Even where loans ultimately refinance, the path almost always involves materially tougher economics.

There were exceptions—e.g., well‑located multifamily with agency or HUD debt could still achieve relatively strong leverage—but the combination of much higher interest rates, reduced LTVs, and tighter underwriting standards meant that **the vast majority of U.S. real estate developers who *needed* to refinance between late 2023 and end‑2024 did so on significantly worse terms than their prior financing, and many could not refinance at all.** That aligns closely with Sacks’s prediction that this problem would "afflict pretty much every" developer facing a refi in that “next year or so,” so the forecast is best judged as *right* in substance, even if the “every” wording is rhetorical rather than literally universal.

predictions.grok_explanation: David Sacks' prediction held true. US CRE faced a massive maturity wall ($929B in 2024 per Huntington Leeds Oct 2024 report), with developers needing to refinance low-rate loans (3-5%) into much higher rates (>7%, e.g., 7.85-8.79% fixed Q1 2024 per Tidalloans). Lenders tightened terms: new LTV ratios fell (50-65% vs prior 65-75%, Benefit Street Partners & Huntington), stricter DSCR/debt service, higher yields/spreads (150-300bps over Treasurys), often requiring additional equity/paydowns/collateral for extensions/mods (mods surged to $22B past 12mo May 2024, Huntington). Many couldn't refinance outright (CMBS refinance rate 85% 2024 vs 94% 2023 per KBRA; 41% extended 2023 per Cohen & Steers), facing worse conditions amid falling values. Reports universally confirm (S&P Global, MBA, Trepp, Fed St. Louis). Lending rebounded 16% to $498B (MBA 2025), but gap met via distressed mods/extensions, affirming 'most' encountered significantly worse terms through 2024.

predictions.explanation:
David Sacks’ normalized prediction was that, for at least the near term after August 2023, **significant portions of the commercial real-estate (CRE) debt market would effectively seize up**, with many syndicated CRE loans drawing *no workable bids* from the usual institutional lenders.

Evidence from late‑2023 and 2024 broadly matches that description:

- By mid‑2023, analysts using Trepp data reported that **U.S. commercial real-estate lending had “ground nearly to a halt”**, with outstanding bank CRE debt growing by less than 1% (the weakest since 2014) and CMBS issuance falling to its lowest level since 2011 as lenders pulled back from the sector amid surging bond yields.([businessinsider.nl](https://www.businessinsider.nl/the-commercial-real-estate-market-is-frozen-as-soaring-bond-yields-bring-lending-to-a-halt/?utm_source=openai))
- A 2024 Franklin Templeton institutional note (drawing on Q4 2023 Trepp data) describes a **“lenders embargo”** in CRE debt: regional banks, mortgage REITs, and many private lenders were “no longer offering capital,” and it states bluntly that **“the loan market has ground to a halt”** in the face of a huge refinancing wall and falling property values.([ftinstitutional.com](https://www.ftinstitutional.com/articles/2024/alternatives/challenges-in-cre-debt-a-wall-of-maturity-and-lenders-embargo?utm_source=openai))  That is effectively the situation Sacks was gesturing at—originators sending deals out and getting no acceptable take‑up from their traditional funding base.
- Additional reporting shows the same pattern of **traditional banks retreating from new CRE lending** while trying to shrink or offload existing portfolios. Regional and smaller banks—who hold the bulk of U.S. CRE loans—have been under intense pressure from rate hikes and office stress, constraining their capacity and willingness to fund new deals.([ft.com](https://www.ft.com/content/1f0b2ba2-8e56-485b-8b3c-f8f1babc34f4?utm_source=openai))
- In parallel, large alternative asset managers and private-credit funds (Blackstone, Apollo, LaSalle, PGIM, etc.) **stepped in to buy discounted CRE loans or originate private loans** *because* banks and other conventional lenders were pulling back. Reuters explicitly frames this as big-name funds piling into real-estate debt “as banks retreat,” confirming that the usual bank-led syndication channel had weakened so much that nonbank capital was filling a vacuum rather than competing away spreads.([reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/business/finance/blackstone-buys-2-billion-cre-loans-atlantic-union-bankshares-2025-06-26/?utm_source=openai))

These sources collectively support the core of Sacks’ claim: in the months after August 2023, **large swaths of the CRE debt market—especially transitional/office-heavy and bank-dependent segments—were functionally frozen, with many prospective loans unable to attract acceptable bids from the normal institutional syndicate buyers.** While activity never went literally to zero and specialized private-credit players did transact, the mainstream bank-and-CMBS pipeline behaved very much like a “no-bid” market for a broad set of deals. On that qualitative, directional basis, the prediction is best judged as **right**.

Anecdotal evidence aligns, e.g., June 2023 report of banks/insurers having 'no bid' for CRE assets ([source](https://www.privatedebtinvestor.com/ares-buys-3-5bn-loan-portfolio-from-pacwest/)). predictions.explanation:
Jason Calacanis made two linked claims for the next 6–12 months after August 18, 2023 (i.e., by roughly February–August 2024): (1) Donald Trump would be *out* of the 2024 race, and (2) the GOP primary would become a three‑way contest among Chris Christie, Vivek Ramaswamy, and Ron DeSantis, with Christie and Ramaswamy surging.

**Trump’s status in Feb–Aug 2024**  
In reality, Trump remained the dominant and eventually *only* major Republican candidate:
- Nikki Haley suspended her campaign on March 6, 2024, explicitly leaving Trump as the last major Republican contender in the primary. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/95ab56b68a8eefbbf04ef90f2f00ef29?utm_source=openai))  
- On March 12, 2024, Trump clinched the Republican nomination by surpassing the required delegate threshold. ([forbes.com](https://www.forbes.com/sites/saradorn/2024/03/12/trump-clinches-republican-nomination/?utm_source=openai))  
He was therefore very much an active and leading candidate throughout the entire February–August 2024 window, directly contradicting the prediction that he would be “out of the race.”

**Field composition and ‘three‑horse race’**  
Far from becoming a three‑way race between Christie, Ramaswamy, and DeSantis, all three exited the race early in 2024—and *before* the 6‑month mark (February 18, 2024):
- Chris Christie suspended his campaign on January 10, 2024, citing no viable path to victory. ([theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2024/jan/10/republican-chris-christie-suspends-presidential-bid?utm_source=openai))  
- Vivek Ramaswamy suspended his campaign and endorsed Trump right after the Iowa caucuses in mid‑January 2024. ([cbsnews.com](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/vivek-ramaswamy-drops-out-2024-presidential-race-iowa-caucuses/?utm_source=openai))  
- Ron DeSantis suspended his campaign and endorsed Trump on January 21, 2024. ([cnbc.com](https://www.cnbc.com/2024/01/21/ron-desantis-drops-out-of-2024-presidential-race-.html?utm_source=openai))  
By late January 2024, the realistic race was primarily Trump vs. Nikki Haley, not a Christie–Ramaswamy–DeSantis three‑way.

Polling during late 2023 also shows Trump maintaining enormous national leads while Christie and Ramaswamy remained in single digits; for example, a Fox News national poll had Trump at 62% with DeSantis at 14%, Haley 11%, Ramaswamy 7%, and Christie 3%, and a Monmouth poll similarly found Trump at 58% with Ramaswamy at 4% and Christie at 2%. ([foxnews.com](https://www.foxnews.com/official-polls/fox-news-poll-support-trump-hits-62-gop-primary?utm_source=openai))  This is the opposite of Christie and Ramaswamy “surging” into a top tier that displaces Trump.

Because (a) Trump was still the leading and then presumptive GOP nominee well within the 6–12 month horizon, and (b) the predicted three‑way race among Christie, Ramaswamy, and DeSantis never materialized (all three dropped out early, and none overtook Trump), the prediction is clearly **wrong** rather than inconclusive or ambiguous.

predictions.explanation:
David Sacks argued that the indictments and "lawfare" against Donald Trump would *polarize* the 2024 outcome, so that Trump would either end up back in the White House or effectively in "the big house," rather than fading away with some moderate, low‑stakes outcome.

What actually happened by November 2025:

1. **Trump was re‑elected president in 2024.**  
   Trump won the 2024 U.S. presidential election, defeating Kamala Harris and becoming the 47th president, with 312 electoral votes and roughly 49.8% of the popular vote. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_United_States_presidential_election?utm_source=openai))  
   This is exactly the “White House” side of the dichotomy Sacks described.

2. **He was convicted of felonies but not sentenced to prison.**  
   In New York, Trump was convicted on 34 felony counts of falsifying business records in May 2024, becoming the first former U.S. president convicted of a felony. However, after his election victory, he was sentenced on January 10, 2025, to an *unconditional discharge*—no prison time and no fine. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prosecution_of_Donald_Trump_in_New_York?utm_source=openai))  
   Other major criminal cases (federal election‑obstruction, classified documents, and the Georgia RICO election‑interference case) were dropped or dismissed after his reelection, leaving him with no active criminal prosecutions or prison sentence as of late 2025. ([time.com](https://time.com/7337113/trump-georgia-election-interference-dismissed-legal-cases/?utm_source=openai))

3. **No “intermediate” outcome occurred.**  
   Rather than quietly exiting politics or being sidelined without conviction or nomination, Trump both secured the Republican nomination and won the presidency again, while his one conviction resulted in no incarceration. He is serving as president, not fading from public life. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump_2024_presidential_campaign?utm_source=openai))

Given that Sacks’ core claim was that the legal onslaught would force a *highly polarized* 2024 outcome—either the White House or the big house—and that Trump in fact returned to the White House, the prediction resolves on the “elected president again” branch of his stated either/or and is therefore **right**.

predictions.explanation:
Donald Trump did in fact win the 2024 Republican presidential nomination, validating David Sacks’s prediction that Republican voters and elites rallying around Trump after the indictments would “ensure that he will be the nominee.”

By March 2024, Trump had secured enough delegates to clinch the Republican nomination after dominating the GOP primary contests, and major Republican leaders and institutions coalesced around his candidacy, with prominent rivals suspending their campaigns and endorsing him. This consolidation of party support confirmed that, despite (and in many analyses partly because of) his indictments, Trump became the clear and ultimately successful frontrunner for the 2024 Republican presidential nomination.

Because the prediction was specifically about *winning the 2024 Republican nomination* (not the general election or broader outcomes), and that has already occurred, the prediction should be scored as **right**.
predictions.grok_explanation: Donald Trump secured the 2024 Republican presidential nomination, clinching it mathematically on March 12, 2024, after winning key primaries ([PBS News](https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/trump-clinches-2024-republican-nomination), [Politico](https://www.politico.com/news/2024/03/12/donald-trump-clinches-republican-presidential-nomination-00146675)), and was officially nominated at the Republican National Convention on July 15, 2024 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Republican_National_Convention), [CBS News](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/rnc-roll-call-of-states-2024/)). This fulfills the prediction made in August 2023 amid his indictments.

predictions.explanation:
Jason Calacanis predicted that, during the 2024 election cycle, the Republican Party would "cut ties" with Donald Trump and effectively expel him as a party leader. In reality, the institutional GOP did the opposite.

By March 2024, the Republican National Committee (RNC) installed Trump-endorsed Michael Whatley as chair and Trump’s daughter-in-law Lara Trump as co-chair, moves widely described as consolidating Trump’s control over party machinery. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Republican_National_Committee_leadership_elections?utm_source=openai))  
At the July 2024 Republican National Convention in Milwaukee, delegates formally selected Donald Trump as the Republican Party’s 2024 presidential nominee, with an overwhelming majority of delegate votes. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Republican_National_Convention?utm_source=openai))  
According to post-election summaries, under Whatley’s leadership the Republican Party went on to win the presidency and congressional majorities in the 2024 elections, confirming Trump’s continued role as the party’s central standard-bearer rather than someone from whom they had "cut ties." ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Whatley?utm_source=openai))  

Subsequently, in 2025 the RNC again elevated a close Trump ally, Joe Gruters, to chair—with Trump’s explicit backing—further demonstrating that party leadership remained aligned with him instead of expelling or sidelining him. ([washingtonpost.com](https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2025/08/22/republican-national-committee-elects-trump-backed-joe-gruters-chair/?utm_source=openai))  

While a few individual Republicans, such as Will Hurd and Senator Lisa Murkowski, publicly refused to support Trump, these were isolated cases and did not constitute the Republican Party as an institution breaking with or expelling him. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Will_Hurd?utm_source=openai))  

Because the GOP not only failed to expel Trump but reaffirmed him as nominee and leader, this prediction turned out to be **wrong**.
